title: Memorize one
hook: the tradition of carrying hadith by heart: why al-Nawawi cut the chains from his forty
tomorrow: one hadith, by heart. now: who gets to pass it on?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the forty as a life: the why at the start, a door left open at the end. A life in forty. Today, a strange choice al-Nawawi made.

Every one of the forty-two is a search away. Type two words and the whole hadith appears, with the chain of who heard it from whom. So here's an odd detail in al-Nawawi's introduction. The chain is the thing hadith scholars check most carefully; a report stands or falls on it. And al-Nawawi says he left the chains out. On purpose. Why would a careful scholar cut the very part his field is built to check?
screen: `A SEARCH AWAY.` → `THE CHAIN: WHO HEARD IT FROM WHOM.` → `HE LEFT THE CHAINS OUT.`

segments.voice: He tells us why: so they'd be easier to memorize. He wasn't writing for a shelf. He was writing for a head. The chains still sit in the big collections, and he names the collection after each hadith, so anyone can check. But the version he handed on was light enough to carry. That's an old habit in this tradition. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, in a report Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi record, in paraphrase: may Allah brighten the face of someone who hears a saying from us, keeps it in memory, and passes it on as he heard it. Then a twist: perhaps the one who carries knowledge carries it to someone who understands it better than he does. So the one who memorizes doesn't have to be the expert. The job is to keep it whole and hand it over. A phone keeps the words. Memory keeps them with you: in the car, in a hard conversation, at two in the morning with no signal and nobody to ask. The Arabic for memorizing is hifz, and a hafiz is someone who holds the whole Qur'an by heart. One hadith is a much smaller start. Something to tell a friend tonight: al-Nawawi trimmed his forty so they'd fit in a memory.
screen: `SO THEY'D BE EASY TO MEMORIZE.` · `MAY ALLAH BRIGHTEN THAT FACE.` · `THE CARRIER NEEDN'T BE THE EXPERT.` · `HIFZ: KEPT, AND CARRIED.` · then, large: `ONE, BY HEART.`

segments.voice: Pick one of the forty, the shortest one you like: don't be angry, or actions are by intentions. Say it out loud three times, then cover it and say it once without looking. For the sit, keep repeating it softly, until it comes without reaching.
Memorize one: carry a single hadith by heart, whole and as you heard it, so it goes wherever you go.
For the road: one, by heart, the part a phone can't do for you. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1472 COUNTS.` → `THE FORTY, GATHERED · 2 OF 3 · YEAR FIVE, 46 OF 365.` → `TOMORROW: ONE HADITH, BY HEART. NOW: WHO GETS TO PASS IT ON?`

howItsDone: Muslim children and adults often memorize hadith alongside the Qur'an, repeating a short report aloud until it comes without looking; al-Nawawi's forty is a common first collection to learn by heart.

chat.says: dadi's said the same du'a every night since forever. i want it memorized before Chicago. too late?
options: Not too late. Learn it from her, a line a night, and say it back to her.
Just save a voice memo of her. Same thing, and you'll never get it wrong.
Learn the whole book of du'as first; one alone won't really count.
chat.meaning: The Prophet blessed whoever hears a saying, keeps it in memory, and passes it on as heard. A phone keeps words; memory carries them.
